opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's actually one of the more interesting questions, because a lot of the most valuable environments people build are going to stay private. If you're a company with a specific workflow or proprietary data, you're not going to publish that, and you shouldn't have to.

But the hub isn't only about sharing the environment itself. A big part of the value is standardization. If everyone writes environments against the same interface, with the same way of defining datasets, rollouts, rubrics, and tool use, then all the infrastructure around it just works. You can plug your private environment into the same trainers, the same eval harnesses, and the same inference setups that everyone else uses. You're not rebuilding the plumbing every time.

The second piece is that the public environments become building blocks. Even if your final environment is private, you're probably not starting from zero. Maybe you take an existing coding environment, or a tool-use harness, or a rubric pattern someone already figured out, and then you swap in your own data or your own reward logic. The open ecosystem gives you a set of well-tested components, and you compose your private thing on top.

There's also the evaluation side. Being able to run your model against a broad suite of public environments, alongside your private ones, gives you a much better picture of whether you're improving on what you care about without regressing on everything else.

So I think of it a bit like open source software in general. Most companies run plenty of private code, but they all benefit enormously from shared libraries, shared conventions, and a shared community figuring out best practices. Environments are heading the same way. The private stuff is where your edge is, but the public layer is what makes building that private stuff cheap and fast.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people miss about the hub is that the value isn't really about publishing. It's about the interface. If you've built your environment against the same spec that everyone else is using, you get a bunch of stuff for free even if nobody else ever sees your code.

The first thing is tooling. Every trainer that speaks the environment protocol just works with your environment. You don't have to write glue code for each new RL framework, you don't have to re-implement your reward function three times because someone wants to try a different training stack. The environment is a package, it has a known shape, and the whole ecosystem of trainers, evals, and inference backends plugs into it.

The second thing is that most teams who keep stuff private still want to share internally. A hub is basically a package registry. You can run your own private index, your research org can push environments to it, and someone on a different team can pull it down and train against it without a two-week onboarding call. That's the same reason people use private PyPI mirrors or private container registries. Nobody thinks those are useless just because the packages aren't public.

And then third, honestly, the public environments are useful as building blocks even if your real work is private. Your proprietary environment is probably some domain-specific thing, but you still want to mix in math, code, instruction following, tool use, whatever, so the model doesn't regress on the general stuff while you're training it on your thing. If those are already packaged in the same format, you compose them. You don't rebuild them.

So I'd frame it as: the hub is where the public ones live, but the real product is the standard. Private environments benefit from the standard just as much as public ones do. Maybe more, because the people building private environments are usually the ones who actually have a training run on the other end.

astra-6.text:
Even if you keep the environments themselves private, there’s a lot of value in having a shared interface for them. How do you interact with an environment? How do you run an agent against it, collect trajectories, and get rewards back? Everyone shouldn’t have to rebuild that infrastructure.

So I think of a hub as more than a place where you publish environments. It can also give you the tooling to develop and run private environments, and let you use the same training infrastructure across public and private ones. You can share the plumbing without sharing the task or the data that makes it valuable to your business.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of value in having a shared interface, even if the environments themselves are private. You can build an environment internally and use the same tooling to train against it, evaluate models, and manage the infrastructure without publishing your tasks or your data.

And a public hub gives you a place to get started. You can try environments, understand what works, and then bring that workflow into your own domain. So the value isn’t just in sharing the environments; it’s also in sharing the machinery around them.
